Photograph: James Ross/AAP New South Wales Man shot dead in Sydney community centre car park NSW police say a vehicle was seen driving away from the scene in Punchbowl in the city’s south-west Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.14 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 06.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has been shot dead in the car park of a Sydney community centre in the city’s south-west. Emergency services were called to the community centre on Rossmore Avenue in Punchbowl on Wednesday evening after reports of a shooting. A vehicle was seen driving away from the location after the fatal shooting, NSW police said in a statement. Paramedics treated the man but he died at the scene. He is yet to be identified, police said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The fatal shooting comes two days after the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced measures to curb gangland violence in Sydney. New laws being introduced in the state include new aggravated offences for conspiracy to commit gang-related murder. The maximum penalty will be increased to life imprisonment. The government has repeatedly denied criminal gangs are “out of control” in the city after the mistaken identity shootings of electrician Joshua Macdonald and Marco Tapia, a 23-year-old biomedical engineering student last week . Police said neither man had any link to organised crime. The new laws being introduced in NSW aim to tackle organised crime by giving police more power, including using new interim serious crime prevention orders to restrict people suspected of serious and organised crime. Those would be applied while the state’s supreme court considers the full order. Children’s indictable offences would include activities linked to organised crime, and public shootings and firebombings would be added to the scheme. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion In a statement on Monday, Minns said people who conspire to arrange a gangland murder should face the prospect of “spending the rest of your life behind bars”. “We want to hit these criminal networks at every point – the people who organise the violence, the people who facilitate it online and the people who ultimately carry it out,” he said. Police are urging anyone with information about the Punchbowl incident to contact Campsie police station or Crime Stoppers. https://www.dw.com/en/german-police-prob.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mrgc Police worked to gather evidence at the scene Image: Christoph Petersen/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Prosecutors in the German city of Wuppertal said on Friday that they had taken over the lead in investigations into an attempted arson attack at the local synagogue. They said a 37-year-old Afghan national arrested near the scene soon after made "comments that indicated an antisemitic motive" to detaining officers. A search of his apartment uncovered weapons. The suspect is being investigated for attempted aggravated arson. He was set to appear before a judge at an arraignment hearing on Friday. What did prosecutors say about the incident and the investigation? The attack took place midafternoon on Thursday. The suspect allegedly threw three containers of flammable liquid at a stairwell and doorway serving as an entrance to the synagogue and its adjoining eatery, Cafe Negev, and then set it alight. The fire was quickly extinguished by a staff member, meaning that nobody was hurt and the damage to the structure was minimal, according to police. "Shortly after, police officers on security duty on site were able to provisionally arrest a 37-year-old man in the immediate vicinity of the crime scene," Wuppertal's prosecutor's office said in a statement. "After reviewing the video surveillance footage from the scene he is strongly suspected of having laid the fire." The attack did not cause much damage as the fire was noticed and swiftly extinguished by staff Image: Matthias Rosenkranz/dpa/picture alliance Although "intensive" background investigations were ongoing, prosecutors said there were already clues regarding the motive. "During the police intervention, he issued comments that indicated an antisemitic motive for the crime," prosecutors wrote. The Wuppertal resident with Afghan citizenship had a prior criminal record for threatening a female neighbor, they said. "His apartment was already searched ... yesterday evening," prosecutors wrote. "Alongside documents several knives and a machete were located, which had been positioned in easy reach." Police were investigating data from the suspect's mobile phone, which they confiscated in the arrest. Police were stationed nearby amid increased security measures at Jewish sites in Germany and could rapidly apprehend a suspect Image: Christoph Petersen/dpa/picture alliance Central Council of Jews in Germany condemns nature of broad-daylight attack Regional broadcaster WDR reported that about 30 people attended an impromptu gathering outside the synagogue on Thursday evening in a show of solidarity. The Central Council of Jews in Germany condemned the attack in the buildup to the Yom Kippur religious holiday on September 20 and 21. "Once again an attack on a synagogue has taken place at the time of Jewish high holidays," said Josef Schuster, the council's president. "What disturbs me most is how coolly the perpetrator in Wuppertal carried out this attack in broad daylight. There's no sign of a sense of shame or being conscious of wrongdoing." Wuppertal, home to around 350,000 people, lies just east of Düsseldorf in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia . https://www.dw.com/en/suspected-pneumoni.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nm2x Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement What you need to know about plague There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic. Bubonic plague is the most common form, it does not spread from person to person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure. If the the bacteria reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is highly contagious as it can pass from person to person through the air, via coughing, for example. If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment. Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community. Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information. Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube. She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia. According to official Russian figures, two hospitals and a children's clinic were placed under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections. The 28-year-old lab worker died in a hospital near Irkutsk Image: Kirill Kukhmar/TASS/picture alliance Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures." Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection All that is known for certain, at time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious. Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis , a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them. The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague. Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics. Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood. A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs. What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague? Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic. All are caused by the same bacterium. What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is. Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people. The bacteria Yersenia pestis is responsible for the plague Image: James Cavallini/BSIP/picture alliance If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first. Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment. Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms. Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill. Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says. Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague. The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers. Poland’s competition authority said on Monday it suspects Google, a unit of Alphabet, of misusing its dominant market position. The concern centers on how the company negotiated payments for content with local media publishers. UOKiK, Poland’s antitrust and consumer protection body, said the charges concern how Google negotiates payments. The payments are for displaying articles and snippets across search results, Google News, and Discover services. This makes the Poland Google antitrust case a key test of how digital platforms pay news publishers.
